😔 Regrets? I Have a Few…
B2 · 1-to-1 · 65–75 min · Grammar + Speaking + Vocabulary
Stage 1 · 8–10 min

Warmer: My Regrets

Exercises 1 & 2 — Personal statements + discussion

Ex 1 is a personal warm-up — student writes first, then shares. Don't correct language at this stage. Ex 2 flows naturally from their answers. Push for developed responses (3–5 sentences). Key question for B2: "Is there a difference between regretting doing something vs. not doing something?"
✏️ Exercise 1 — Complete the statements about yourself
  • 💭 I regret not… earlier.
  • 💭 The decision I regret the most is…
  • 💭 In the future I might regret… if I don't change anything about…
  • 💭 I used to regret… but now I've come to terms with it.

Click a question to highlight it:

Stage 2 · 10 min

Speaking: Who Regrets What?

Exercises 3 & 4 — Categorise + watch a short video

Student categorises each regret BEFORE watching. Encourage them to explain their reasoning. After clicking, discuss disagreements — there are no strictly "correct" answers. Then play the video in two parts as indicated. The video checks Ex 3 answers. If time is short, skip the video and move on.
🗂 Exercise 3 — Whose regret is it? Click to categorise

b) not take more advantage of their college experience
c) tease their sister or brother
d) not follow their dreams earlier in life
e) get angry at their family

g) not say sorry more often

🎬 Exercise 4 — Watch and check your answers
▶ Part 1: 0:00 – 1:00 ▶ Part 2: 1:47 – 2:38

After watching, discuss: Were your predictions correct? Which regrets surprised you most?

Stage 3 · 8–10 min

Opinions: How Much Do You Agree?

Exercise 5 — Rate each statement 0 to 3, then discuss

Student rates each statement, then explains their rating with reasons. Push for B2-level justification — ask "Can you give an example?" or "Do you think this is always true?" Statements 3, 4, and 6 tend to spark the best debates. Teacher rates too, and compare.
📊 Exercise 5 — Rate each statement. Give reasons!
0 = Disagree 1 = Partly agree 2 = Agree 3 = Absolutely agree
"The older you get, the fewer things you tend to regret."
"If you listen to the regrets older people have, you are likely to avoid their mistakes."
"Regretting too many things is meaningless — we can't change the past."
"If you focus on your regrets, you might overlook new opportunities."
"For some people, their regrets are the only thing they have — it's too late for them to change anything."
"People who say they don't regret anything are only fooling themselves."
Stage 4 · 10–12 min

Grammar: Expressing Regrets

Exercise 6 — Analyse four structures, same meaning

Ask student to read all four sentences and answer the analysis questions BEFORE showing the grammar boxes. The key insight: all four sentences express the same regret, but with different structures. Focus on verb forms — especially the contrast between regret + -ing (gerund) vs. should have + past participle. If only is stronger/more emotional than I wish.
🔍 Exercise 6 — Read the sentences. Answer the questions below.
Four ways to express the same regret
a)I regret not following my dreams earlier in life.
b)I should have followed my dreams earlier in life.
c)I wish I had followed my dreams earlier in life.
d)If only I had followed my dreams earlier in life.
  • Do all four sentences have the same or different meaning? What's the key difference between them?
  • Are these regrets about something in the present or the past?
  • What verb form comes after regret in sentence (a)? What about should in sentence (b)?
  • What tense is used after I wish and If only? Is there a difference in meaning between (c) and (d)?
🔴 regret + -ing
regret + verb + -ing
"I regret not following my dreams."
Expresses a past action we feel sorry about now. Not is placed before the gerund to express a regret about not doing something.
🟡 should have + past participle
should / shouldn't have + V3
"I should have followed my dreams." / "I shouldn't have given up."
Criticises a past decision. Shouldn't have = regret about doing something wrong.
🔵 I wish + past perfect
I wish + had (not) + V3
"I wish I had followed my dreams." / "I wish I hadn't given up."
Expresses regret about past situations. More formal than if only.
🟣 If only + past perfect
If only + had (not) + V3
"If only I had followed my dreams!"
Stronger and more emotional than I wish. Often used with exclamation marks to show deep regret or frustration.
Stage 5 · 12 min

Grammar Practice: Paraphrase

Exercise 7 — Rewrite each regret using the word in brackets

Student writes their version, then clicks to compare with the model. Accept any paraphrase that correctly uses the target structure — model answers are a guide, not the only correct version. Discuss why certain structures feel more or less natural for each situation. Note: (f) is the reverse direction — If only → regret.
✏️ Exercise 7 — Paraphrase the regrets. Use the word in brackets.

Rewrite each sentence keeping the same meaning. Make any other changes necessary. Then click Show model to compare.

  • a
    I regret making this decision without talking to anyone. If I had, everything would have turned out much better.
    should
    ✅ Model answer
    I should have talked to someone before making this decision. If I had, everything would have turned out much better.
  • b
    I shouldn't have taken a taxi to work. With all these traffic jams, I'm going to be late.
    wish
    ✅ Model answer
    I wish I hadn't taken a taxi to work. With all these traffic jams, I'm going to be late.
  • c
    I regret lying to them in the first place. Now I'm lost and have no idea what to do next.
    only
    ✅ Model answer
    If only I hadn't lied to them in the first place. Now I'm lost and have no idea what to do next.
  • d
    I should have spent more time preparing for this exam. Then, I would have got a better result.
    wish
    ✅ Model answer
    I wish I had spent more time preparing for this exam. Then, I would have got a better result.
  • e
    I regret moving to the countryside. There's so little to do apart from work and I feel bored most of the time.
    should
    ✅ Model answer
    I shouldn't have moved to the countryside. There's so little to do apart from work and I feel bored most of the time.
  • f
    If only I had never said that to her. She'll never forgive me!
    regret
    ✅ Model answer
    I regret saying that to her. She'll never forgive me!
Stage 6 · 10 min

Vocabulary: Responding to Regrets

Exercises 8 & 9 — Gap fill + matching

Ex 8 — student selects the word from the drop-down, then check together. Make sure the student can produce the full phrase naturally (e.g. "be hard on yourself" not just "hard"). Ex 9 — pairs responses with regrets from Ex 7. Discuss: which response would be most useful to hear? Which is least helpful?
💬 Exercise 8 — Complete the responses using the words in the box
Word bank
feel
hard
look
prone
pull
take
  1. Don't be so on yourself. You did your best.
  2. Why don't you try and yourself together? It's going to be OK. We'll be on time.
  3. If I were you, I wouldn't it so seriously. You can always apologise for what you said.
  4. I wish you could on the bright side. This place is so beautiful! Besides, you can visit the city whenever you want.
  5. I you on this one. But it doesn't mean there's no way out.
  6. All of us are to mistakes. Learn from this lesson and reach out for someone next time.

Select which response (1–6) best fits each regret (a–f). Think about the situation!

Regrets (from Ex 7)
a Made a decision without talking to anyone

Stage 7 · 10–12 min

Role Play: What Are They Saying?

Exercise 10 — Use regret structures + response phrases

Click a card to reveal the role prompts. Student and teacher take turns playing the roles. Student should use at least two different structures for expressing regrets across all situations, and at least three different response phrases. Encourage improvisation — the prompts are a starting point, not a script.
🗣 Useful language — use these in the role plays
I regret + -ing…
I should have…
I wish I had/hadn't…
If only I had/hadn't…
Don't be hard on yourself
Look on the bright side
Pull yourself together
I feel you
Be prone to mistakes
Don't take it so seriously

Click a situation card to see the role prompts. Then act it out!

1 👩‍❤️‍👩
💬 Speaker (expressing regret)
"I said something awful in that argument. I should never have… If only I had…"
🤝 Listener (responding)
Comfort them. Use at least two response phrases. Ask what they plan to do now.
2 📚😣
💬 Speaker (expressing regret)
"I really regret not studying harder. I wish I had… I should have…"
🤝 Listener (responding)
You failed too! Share your own regret and encourage each other. What will you do differently next time?
3 👩‍⚕️😔
💬 Speaker (patient — regretting)
"I regret not coming sooner. If only I had… I should have listened when…"
🤝 Listener (doctor — responding)
Be reassuring but honest. Use response phrases and explain what can still be done.
4 👴👵😟
💬 One partner (regretting)
"I wish we hadn't… If only we had stayed in… I sometimes regret not…"
🤝 Other partner (responding)
You partly agree, but see things differently. Respond with both empathy and optimism.
5 🎬😭
💬 Speaker (upset partner)
"I wish I hadn't agreed to see this film… I should have insisted on… If only we had chosen…"
🤝 Listener (the one who picked the film)
You also feel guilty. Express your own regret and try to cheer them up. Keep it light!
6 🧑‍🏫😞
💬 Young person (regretting)
"I regret dropping out. I should have listened… If only I had continued… I wish I had…"
🤝 Mentor (responding)
Be supportive but motivating. Use response phrases and ask about what they could still do now.

🎉 Lesson complete!

You've covered 4 structures for expressing regrets, 6 response phrases, and used them all in real conversation. See you next time — hopefully with no regrets! 😄
